title: Players Returning from Achilles, ACL and Other Major Injuries
brief: What should we expect from players coming back from Achilles tears, ACL tears and other major injuries: timelines, efficiency loss, minutes limits and skipped back-to-backs? It must say how to price them in our H2H league and why the market is often too scared of them.
summary: Players coming back from Achilles and ACL tears usually return close to their old level, but year one brings lower efficiency, minutes limits and skipped back-to-backs. The draft market is often too scared of them. In our 9-cat H2H auction, bid above their market price but below their healthy value, check whether the timeline puts them on the court by the playoffs (weeks 19 to 21, ending 2027-03-28), and plan to cover the games they sit.

sections.heading: Timelines: when they actually come back

paragraphs.text: A full Achilles tear usually takes 9 to 12 months to recover from, and most cases lean toward 12. A partial tear can take about 6 months. A full 12 months or more off may help a player come back stronger than a 9 to 11 month return. So do not treat a slow return as bad news.

A normal ACL return takes about 12 months. A player more than 12 months past a torn ACL can be treated as fully healthy. Today is 2026-10-16. That means an ACL tear from before mid-October 2025 should be a non-issue by opening night. Players whose game is built on IQ and strength come back from an ACL better than speed-based players like Zach LaVine.

Before you bid, check the date against our calendar. Our playoffs run in weeks 19, 20 and 21, roughly 2027-03-08 to 2027-03-28. The trade deadline is 2027-03-04. Add 12 months to the tear date for a full Achilles or ACL tear. If that date lands after early March 2027, the player probably gives you little before or during our playoffs. Price him as a cheap stash at most.

sections.heading: What the first season back looks like

paragraphs.text: Expect lower efficiency in year one. Players coming back from ACL or Achilles tears almost always lose efficiency in their first season. Achilles returnees lose it mostly on two-point shots and finishing. In our league that hits FG% hardest. FG% is a team ratio, so a high-volume player who finishes worse can pull down your whole team's percentage.

Expect minutes limits and missed back-to-backs. ACL returnees usually have their minutes managed and sit out back-to-backs early on. Achilles returnees rarely play both games of a back-to-back. In the last 10 years basically only Wes Matthews did it, and he played heavily reduced minutes in the second game. Older returnees will likely sit back-to-backs early in the season too.

The hidden cost goes beyond missed games. While a player ramps back up on limited minutes, all of his counting stats drop: points, rebounds, assists, steals, blocks and threes. For a 9-cat team, a capped player gives you a smaller share in every category, not just one.
Watch for knock-on injuries. Achilles returnees carry a risk of compensation injuries elsewhere in the body. After major lower-body surgery, soreness on the other side from compensating is common.

On how much these players lose, one view says recent Achilles returnees have mostly come back close to their old level. It says the old rule of a permanent 10% drop in production no longer holds. The other view says players coming back from ACL or Achilles tears almost always lose efficiency in their first season. Both can be true. Plan for a dip in FG% this season, but do not discount the player as if he lost a career's worth of value.

On durability, one note warns that some players lose production for a long time after even a minor injury, so injury-prone players can hurt you for longer than the injury itself. It also flags compensation injury risk after an Achilles. Another note says compensation soreness after lower-body surgery is common and does not by itself make a player injury-prone. Treat a single major tear as a one-time event. Save the bigger discount for players with a long history of injuries.

On back-to-back schedules, one note says returnees may sit back-to-backs, so teams with many back-to-backs hurt them more. Another says back-to-back counts matter mostly for injury-prone players. A third says most back-to-back problems come from players returning from in-season injuries, and nobody can predict those. Check the team's back-to-back count for a known returnee from a major injury, because his rest days are predictable. Do not lower a healthy player's price for his schedule.

sections.heading: How to price them in our auction

paragraphs.text: The market is often too scared. Drafters overreact to players who missed last season with injuries, and you can be more confident than their draft position suggests. Older prospects who missed their rookie year to injury also get bumped down. These are the spots where the room's fear gives you value.

Use a simple rule on 2026-10-18. Start from the player's healthy value. Cut it for the games he will sit: missed back-to-backs and any early-season minutes cap. Cut a bit more if he is a high-volume two-point scorer, because the efficiency dip lands on FG%. Bid up to that number, even when the room has stopped bidding below it. Players more than 12 months past an ACL tear need almost no discount.

Lean toward players who are strength and IQ based. Be more careful with speed-based players. Give a bit more credit to Achilles returnees who took a full 12 months or more. If the 12-month mark lands after the trade deadline or in our playoffs, keep the player to an end-game bid. Only 144 players get drafted, so a late stash costs you little.
Do not stack too many of them. Each one sits on back-to-backs. With only 2 bench spots and daily lineups, you can cover one or two players' rest nights. You cannot cover four or five.
Set lineups every day. Expect Achilles returnees to sit one game of most back-to-backs. Fill that slot from your bench or with a FAB pickup. Remember the limit of 6 acquisitions per week.
Use the other side of the trade. When an older returnee sits a back-to-back, his backup gets more games. Those backups are good short-term waiver adds, especially early in the season.

Hold, and look for trades. Minutes limits ease as the player ramps up, so his value should be higher in the second half than in October. Managers who sell after slow early box scores give you a chance to buy before the 2027-03-04 deadline. Be quicker to sell a player whose history shows long slumps after minor injuries.
